hook.what_happens: A side-by-side comparison of a woman's face labeled 'Before' and 'After' asks 'What else changed?'
hook.why_it_works: It challenges the viewer's perception of standard cosmetic surgery results.

narrative_arc: Introduce the illusion of before/after plastic surgery photos.
Identify the four key photographic variables.
Demonstrate the impact of lighting changes.
Demonstrate the impact of camera distance.
Demonstrate the impact of head tilt.
Demonstrate the impact of facial expression.
Conclude that photos cannot be separated from the surgery itself.
Provide a call to action to try the experiment or search for Refina AI.

onscreen_text.text: One of these is before surgery. One is after. Watch what else changed.
In most before-and-afters, the surgery isn't the only thing that moved. Four other things
One. The light. Flat light from the front erases most of the shadow on a face. Move it overhead and the folds and hollows come straight back. Same face, nothing touched.
Two. The distance. A phone at arm's length pushes the nose forward and pulls the jaw in. Two steps back, and the whole face rebalances, with nothing done to it.
Three. The tilt. Chin down hides a jawline. Chin level gives you one. That's a few degrees.
Four. The face you're making. A relaxed mouth and a slight lift move the midface before anyone has touched it.
None of this means the surgery did nothing. It means you can't separate the surgery from the photograph by looking at it. Both are true at
So test it yourself. Two photos, same room, a minute apart. Light in front, then light above. You'll meet two different people.
1 Two photos, same room, a minute apart.
2 One with the light in front of you.
3 One with the light above you.
The only comparison worth anything is the same face, same light, same lens, same angle. Ask any gallery for that. Or see it on your own face first.
